US Imposes Broad Tariffs on Cypriot Imports, Hitting Key Sectors

The United States this week imposed sweeping tariffs on a range of imports from Cyprus, prompting concerns among Cypriot exporters and policymakers over the potential impact on the island’s economy. The new measures, announced Monday, introduce tariffs of up to 25% on Cypriot cement, agricultural goods, pharmaceuticals, and manufactured products, in what US officials described as a response to “unresolved trade imbalances and compliance issues.”

The move has sent ripples through Cyprus’s export sector, as the US represents one of the country’s largest non-EU trading partners. Among the companies affected is Vassiliko Cement Works Ltd, a major producer and exporter whose shipments to US buyers have been disrupted.

“This tariff regime poses a significant challenge to our operations,” said Andreas Georgiou, spokesperson for Vassiliko Cement Works Ltd. “We are already seeing delays in contracts and uncertainty among our US customers.”

The Cyprus Chamber of Commerce and Industry estimated that the tariffs could affect over €120 million in annual exports. “This will have a knock-on effect, not just for exporters but for related industries across Cyprus,” said Eleni Sofroniou, the Chamber’s international trade director. “We urge diplomatic efforts to resolve this swiftly.”

Local manufacturers such as Medilife Pharma and Mediterranean Agrofoods have also reported difficulties, with orders put on hold as US importers reassess pricing and supply chains. The Cyprus Ministry of Energy, Commerce and Industry said it is in contact with US officials and EU counterparts, seeking a resolution.

Analysts warn that if the dispute continues, Cypriot producers may be forced to seek alternative markets, potentially at lower margins. “The broader risk is to investor and business confidence,” said economist Nicos Charalambous. “A protracted trade dispute could dampen economic growth in 2024.”
